drop.title: Three Ways to Corner a Root, and the Speed They Cost

title: Three Ways to
Corner a Root
slides.dek: Bisection, the secant method, and Newton all chase the same zero. Race them on one equation and their convergence orders, 1, the golden ratio, and 2, separate into three visibly different slopes.

slides.body: You have a function and you want where it crosses zero. For most equations worth asking there is no formula, so you guess, measure how wrong you are, and guess better; every root-finder is a rule for that second step. *Bisection* keeps two points that straddle the root and halves the gap between them: it cannot fail, but each step buys just one more bit. *The secant* forgets the bracket, draws a line through your last two guesses and jumps to where it hits the axis, faster, but free to wander off and miss. *Newton* slides down the tangent from your guess, fastest of the three, doubling its correct digits each step. On Newton's own cubic, to twelve digits: bisection needs 37 steps, the secant 6, Newton 5.

Counting steps is crude. The honest measure is *order*: if your error this step is e, a method has order p when the next error behaves like e raised to the power p. Order 1 just multiplies the error by a fixed fraction, which is bisection, always by one half. Order 2 squares it, the digit-doubling that makes Newton famous. To read p off real data, take logarithms: the log of one error against the log of the last falls on a straight line whose *slope is the order*. Plotted that way, bisection sits on slope 1, Newton on slope 2, and the secant on a slope of about *1.618*, the golden ratio φ, because each of its guesses leans on the previous two errors and the balancing exponent is the root of p² = p + 1.

slides.sub: Step bisection, the secant, and Newton in lockstep on one equation and watch the gap open: 37 steps, 6, and 5 to the same twelve digits. Then plot each method's errors log against log and read its convergence order straight off the slope, 1 for bisection, 2 for Newton, and φ ≈ 1.618, the golden ratio, for the secant. Switch to arctan from a wide start and watch Newton fling itself out of the number system while bisection keeps closing. Then meet Brent's method, the hybrid under scipy's brentq that keeps the guarantee and steals the speed.
